result:
There is a very specific kind of quiet that happens right before a heavy rain. It’s not just the absence of sound; it’s a holding of breath. The air turns the color of a bruised plum, the wind shifts direction with a sudden, nervous energy, and every bird in the neighborhood vanishes all at once. The world stops talking to itself and waits. 

I’ve always liked those moments. They remind us that nature isn’t just a backdrop for our lives—it’s an active, breathing entity that occasionally demands our full attention. You can be inside, completely lost in the glow of a screen or the mundanity of folding laundry, but when *that* sky appears, you drop everything. You walk to the window. You open it just an inch to smell the petrichor—that sharp, dusty scent of dry earth meeting moisture—and for a minute or two, your internal monologue just shuts off.

It makes you think about how much of our lives we spend insulated from the elements. We live in climate-controlled boxes, insulated by drywall, double-paned glass, and noise-canceling headphones. We’ve done a magnificent job of making ourselves comfortable, buffering against the extremes of the world. 

Yet, we still crave the raw edges. Why else do people flock to the coast during a gale, or sit in awe of a bonfire, or travel thousands of miles just to stare at a canyon? We look for things that dwarf us. We need reminders that the universe is vast, indifferent, and wildly beautiful, entirely unconcerned with our deadlines or our grocery lists.

Lately, I’ve been wondering if we don't treat our inner lives the same way we treat our physical environments. We insulate our minds, too. We scroll through feeds that soothe us, avoid awkward conversations, curate our playlists so we never have to sit in the jarring silence of our own thoughts. We build emotional double-paned glass.

And then a storm hits—a grief, a sudden change, a moment of profound clarity—and we remember that we are porous. We were built to feel the pressure drop. 

Maybe that’s why storms are cathartic. They give us permission to be overwhelmed. They take the ambient anxiety of daily existence and give it shape, sound, and a timeline. It’s going to pour for twenty minutes, the thunder will rattle the panes, and then the clouds will break, leaving behind an exaggerated, washed-clean green world where the light hits the pavement just a little bit brighter.

The rain is starting now. Just a few heavy, hesitant drops hitting the tin flashing outside, like someone tapping a finger on a desk. The air is cooling down. I think I'll close the laptop, open the window a little wider, and just watch it come down.
